name: Anemic vs Rich Domain Models
intent: Decide where the rules of a business object live: in services that operate on bare data, or in the object that owns the data, so that it cannot be put into a state the business forbids; and recognise when plain data is the right answer.
scenario: An Order has four rules: ship only when paid, ship only when not empty, add no items after shipping, and a discount of at most 50%. Five code paths each try all four forbidden changes, 20 attempts in all. Three go through an OrderService (checkout, REST controller, nightly job) and two write fields directly (a support admin tool, a CSV import job). The same code is built as an anemic model, a model that is rich where rules exist, and a model that is rich everywhere. A plain Country lookup table is then given the same treatment.
problem: In an anemic model the objects are bags of fields with getters and setters, and the rules live in separate services. Nothing stops code that does not go through the service from setting a field directly, so every rule is only as strong as the discipline of every caller, and a new rule must be written in each place that sidesteps the old ones. Martin Fowler called this an anti-pattern in 2003 because it keeps the syntax of objects and loses the point of them. The opposite error is to push everything into the entity, persistence and email included, until it cannot be tested without a database, and to build rich objects for plain tables that have no rules at all.

howItWorks.title: Find the invariants first
howItWorks.text: An invariant is a statement that must always be true of an object: an order cannot be shipped unless it is paid and non-empty, nothing is added once it has shipped, a discount is at most 50%. Write them down before choosing a model. If the list is empty or trivial, the thing is data, and the rest of this page about protecting it is not needed.

howItWorks.title: Anemic: rules in services, data in bags
howItWorks.text: The Order has public fields and the OrderService has ship, addItem and applyDiscount with the checks. The checkout service, the REST controller and the nightly job call the service and are safe. The admin tool and the CSV import write the fields directly, and all four forbidden changes get in through each of them: 8 of the 20 attempts succeed. The rules are not wrong; they are optional.

howItWorks.title: Rich: the object guards its own state
howItWorks.text: In the rich Order the fields are private and the only ways to change it are methods that check the rules: ship refuses an unpaid or empty order, addItem refuses a shipped one, applyDiscount refuses 80. All 5 callers go through those methods because there is no other way in, and 0 of 20 forbidden changes succeed. A new rule, no discount on a shipped order, is written in 1 place, where in the anemic version it is 3: the service and each caller that bypasses it.

howItWorks.title: Enforce at the boundary of a consistency unit
howItWorks.text: In domain-driven design the invariant is protected by an aggregate, a cluster of objects that must change together, such as the order and its lines, and outside code may change it only through one entity, the aggregate root. Rules that span several aggregates, or need data from outside, belong in a domain service, which is still behaviour in the model and not an anemic service. Rich does not mean one huge class; it means the rule lives next to the data it guards.

howItWorks.title: Stop at the business rules
howItWorks.text: Rich everywhere gives the entity save(), emailReceipt() and renderInvoice(). It still blocks all 20 forbidden changes, but testing one rule now needs a database and a mailer, and the plain Country table, with two fields and no rules, needs 8 methods where 2 were enough and protects nothing more. Keep persistence, messaging and presentation outside the entity: behaviour that is about the business rules belongs inside, the rest does not.

pros: A rich object cannot be put into a forbidden state, whoever calls it: the rule is mandatory, not a convention
A rule is written once, next to the data it protects, so a new rule is a one-place change
The domain language shows up in method names (ship, applyDiscount), which reads like the business
Rules can be tested on the object alone, with no database, no framework and no mocks
cons: More design effort than a bag of fields, and the model has to be learnt by everyone who writes to it
Object-relational mappers and serializers often want public setters and a default constructor, so the framework pushes toward anemic
The line between a rule that belongs in the entity and one that needs outside data takes judgement
A rich model for a table of plain records adds ceremony and no protection
whenToUse: Objects with real invariants: money, orders, accounts, bookings, state machines with allowed transitions
When more than one code path changes the same data (a web app, an import, an admin tool, a job) and all must obey the same rules
When the rules change often, and the cost of finding every place that enforces them is already visible
Domains where the language of the business matters and the code is meant to reflect it
whenNotToUse: Simple CRUD: a lookup table, a settings record or a form with no rules beyond field types and required fields
Data that is just carried between layers or systems (transfer objects, API payloads), where plain data is the point
As a reason to put persistence, email, rendering or HTTP into the entity
Code in a functional style that keeps data and functions apart on purpose, with types that make illegal states unrepresentable; that is a different way to get the same guarantee
pitfalls: Public setters on a class that has rules: the rule is then only enforced by whoever remembers to call the service, and admin tools and imports forget
Declaring the same rule in a service and again in a controller 'to be safe': the two drift apart, and a change to one is missed
Treating anemic as a sin everywhere: a Country or Currency table with no rules gains nothing from behaviour, and the rich version only adds methods
Turning the entity into a god object with save, email and rendering, so that testing a rule needs a database and a mail fake
A getter that hands out the internal list, so callers add to it and bypass addItem; return a read-only view or a copy
Letting the ORM dictate the model: a mapper that needs public setters is a reason to map to a separate persistence type, not to drop the rules
Confusing rich with large: a rich model is many small objects, each guarding its own few rules, not one class with every method

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: A code path that changes orders: checkout, controller, job, admin tool, import.

roles.label: Order service
roles.description: Holds the rules in the anemic design.

roles.label: Order
roles.description: A bag of fields when anemic, a guard of its own rules when rich.

roles.label: Business rules
roles.description: The four invariants that must always hold.

roles.label: Database and mailer
roles.description: Infrastructure that an entity should not need in order to be tested.

quiz.question: Three callers use OrderService.ship, and an admin tool sets order.shipped = true directly. What is the real weakness of the anemic design?
options: The rules are implemented badly in the service.
The rules are optional: any code that skips the service skips them.
The service class has too many methods to read.
The Order class has too few fields to describe an order.
quiz.explanation: The checks in the service are fine, but nothing makes callers use it. A rich Order with private fields makes the rule the only way in, so the admin tool cannot bypass it.

quiz.question: A table of 200 countries has a code and a name and no rules. What does the model suggest?
options: Make each Country rich, so that every entity in the system is modelled the same way.
Add validate, rename and save methods to Country, to prepare for later rules.
Keep it as plain data with a repository: there is no invariant to protect.
Move it into the Order entity, so that all reference data sits in one place.
quiz.explanation: Behaviour is worth having where there are rules to keep. In the simulation, rich-everywhere writes 8 methods for Country where 2 are enough and protects nothing extra.

quiz.question: A rich Order gets save(), emailReceipt() and renderInvoice(). What is the most likely consequence?
options: Testing one rule now needs a database and a mailer.
More forbidden changes get in, since the entity has more methods.
Rules must now be written again in every caller.
The entity can no longer be shared between several callers.
quiz.explanation: The rules are still enforced, with 0 of 20 forbidden changes accepted, but the entity now depends on infrastructure, so its tests need a database and a mailer. Keep persistence and messaging outside.
